extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; critics evaluating Romantic-era poets
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and aesthetic standards for judging poetry and prose of early 19th-century Romantic writers (Byron, Southey, Wordsworth), focusing on style, originality, subject-matter, temperament, and moral/ social attitudes in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry within nature and received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry moves best within the circle of nature and received opinion; speculative theory and subtle casuistry are forbidden ground to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid transporting poetry into abstruse metaphysical or legalistic subtleties; keep verse grounded in natural feeling and commonly received human experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical ornament in verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make metaphysics 'flowery speeches' nor let metaphysical thought 'dance a measure in the fetters of verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical ideas are inappropriate when they become rhetorical show in poetry; reserve verse for feeling and natural expression rather than abstruse theorising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs. superb common-places
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should not be a 'tissue of superb common-places'; paradoxes that are merely 'familiar in the schools' and only striking by being out of place are defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for genuine originality of thought and placement; avoid relying on grand-sounding but clichéd ideas or paradoxes that lack true novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to the spirit of the age
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should not pander to the spirit of the age or go to the very edge of extreme and licentious speculation merely to please or shock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fashionable excesses and provocations designed solely to attract attention; provocation is not a substitute for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and relation to common life
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's social rank or privilege must not lead to pampered egotism or contempt for 'every-day mortals'; the poet should not disdain ordinary people and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain sympathy with common life; genius should not translate into aloofness or hauteur that disconnects verse from general humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using rank as defence for error
rubrics_metrics.description: One's social elevation (e.g., being a 'Noble Poet') must not set censure at defiance or excuse fantastical opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank or celebrity does not excuse poor judgment in thought or style; poets must be prepared for critical scrutiny regardless of station.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries must be impartial and well-formed
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries should not be partial and hasty; conclusions that are 'raw and unconcocted' with an infusion of whim and humour are faults (ascribed to Mr. Southey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting self-opinion, pique, or the charm of novelty drive one's judgments; cultivate patient, impartial inquiry and well-digested conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion, keeping, system in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should have proportion, keeping, system, and standard rules; being 'crude and chaotic, self-opinionated, vain' are defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect structural unity and disciplined craftsmanship; exuberant fancy must be balanced by form and coherence if the work is to succeed as a rule-giver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit subject and form to the poet's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose modes and subjects suited to one's nature (e.g., a 'garland of wild flowers suits' some poets better than laureate-wreaths or courtly presentation-poems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match poetic form and occasion to the writer's strengths; avoid adopting personae or courtly styles alien to the poet's true voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness and variety can justify rule-breaking (conditionally)
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety, boldness, and lively stimulus of a luxuriant fancy may atone for violations of rules, if regarded as natural growth, but not if the author claims to be a law-giver or judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-breaking is defensible when it springs from imaginative richness and does not arrogate prescriptive authority over others' taste or style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose virtues: plainness, clarity, pointedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should be plain, clear, pointed, familiar, modern in texture, perhaps with occasional archaisms — better manner than matter if necessary (praised of Mr. Southey's prose-style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value lucidity and a natural prose manner; playfulness, biting satire, learning and information are desirable qualities in critical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretending to be prescriptive while being irregular
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer who is 'wild, irregular, singular, extreme' should not attempt to enforce uniformity of taste or 'introduce an uniformity of intellectual weights and measures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not condemn others to rules you yourself break; be modest about prescribing standards if your own work exemplifies exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vernacular style and humble subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may adopt a vernacular, popular, inartificial style that relies upon 'household truths' and the simplest elements of nature and human mind (Wordsworth's approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common speech and humble incidents as legitimate material for serious poetry; grandeur can come from depth of feeling, not theatrical diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small incidents as pegs for profound reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Take common, trifling incidents or objects as 'pegs or loops to hang thought and feeling on'; incidents may be small while reflections are profound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let modest events ground larger meditations; do not require epic happenings for serious poetic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strip off theatrical ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the 'trappings of verse' — cloud-capt towers, solemn temples, gorgeous palaces, the harp of Homer, the trump of Pindar — as meretricious, theatrical, and vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return to a 'tabula rasa' of poetry that dispenses with pomp and costume in favour of truth and nature; avoid relying on traditional grandeur as a substitute for genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer subtle, natural imagery over catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer imagery of gentle, natural particulars (dew-drops, rainbows, breeze through fern) to startling horrors like shipwrecks or overwhelming catastrophe to move the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, well-observed natural images can supply living colouring and emotional effect more honestly than contrived spectacle.
